opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, a lot of those projects are really about teaching, even when they don't look like it. Something like the Annotated Transformer started because I wanted to understand the paper myself. The best way I know to understand something is to sit down and implement it line by line, and then write it up so someone else can follow along. That turned out to be really useful to people, because papers often leave out the details that actually matter when you go to build the thing.

The puzzles and MiniTorch come from a similar place. As a field, we've gotten very good at using these libraries, but a lot of people treat PyTorch as a black box. They know how to call the functions, but they don't have a clear mental model of what autodiff is doing, what broadcasting really means, or why some code is fast on a GPU and other code isn't. So I try to make small, self-contained things where you rebuild the core ideas from scratch and run into the same problems the library designers faced.

Then there's a more research-oriented strand, things like Torch-Struct or the named tensor work. Those are about the question of whether the abstractions we have are the right ones. Can we make structured models easier to express? Can we make tensor code less error-prone by being explicit about dimensions? I don't think every one of those ideas has to win, but writing the code is a way of making the argument concrete. You can debate design in the abstract forever, but once there's something people can pip install and try, you learn very quickly whether it helps.

So overall, the purpose is part pedagogy and part arguing about how we should write machine learning code. And honestly, a lot of it is just that I enjoy it. Writing clean code that explains an idea is one of my favorite parts of the job.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing whether PyTorch abstractions are useful, but does not clearly frame the projects as exploring the boundaries of what PyTorch can do.

r002.rationale: It says the puzzles and MiniTorch help people rebuild ideas such as autodiff and broadcasting through small programs, but does not clearly describe learning mathematical topics through hands-on play.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me the projects really serve two purposes, and they're a little in tension with each other.

The first is pedagogical. A lot of what I've put out, things like the annotated Transformer, MiniTorch, the tensor puzzles, came out of teaching. I'd be standing in front of a class trying to explain attention or autograd, and I'd realize that the paper or the library hides the actual mechanism behind a lot of abstraction. So the goal is to strip it down to the point where someone can read every line and say, okay, I actually understand what this does. PyTorch is great for that because it's imperative, the code reads like the math, and you can poke at the tensors in a notebook. I think of those projects less as software and more as executable explanations. If someone can reimplement it in an afternoon, that's success.

The second purpose is more research-oriented, and that's where things like Torch-Struct or the sequence modeling and state space work come in. There the idea is that a certain class of models, structured prediction, dynamic programming over trees or sequences, was really awkward to express in standard deep learning frameworks, and so people just didn't try them. If you build a library that makes those things first-class, differentiable, batched on a GPU, you change what experiments people are willing to run. So the project is partly an argument that this family of models deserves to be in the toolkit, not just a tool.

The tension is that teaching code wants to be tiny and transparent, and research infrastructure wants to be general and fast, and those pull in opposite directions. I've mostly resolved it by being honest about which one a given project is. I'm not trying to build the next big framework. I'm trying to make a specific idea legible, or make a specific class of models easy enough to try that someone who isn't me will do something with it I didn't anticipate. When that happens, when someone sends me a fork that goes somewhere I never would have gone, that's the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response says some projects make structured models easier to express in deep learning frameworks, but it frames their purpose as teaching or research infrastructure rather than exploring the boundaries of PyTorch.

r002.rationale: It identifies tensor puzzles as teaching projects and describes learning by reading, manipulating tensors in notebooks, and reimplementing small programs.

astra-6.text:
I think of them mostly as a way to explain ideas. With something like the Annotated Transformer, the goal is to take a paper that can feel pretty abstract and show how the pieces fit together in code that you can actually run and change. PyTorch is a really nice medium for that because the code can stay fairly close to the math.

And building these projects is also how I learn. If I can turn an idea into a small, readable implementation, that forces me to understand it much more precisely. My hope is that someone else can pick it up, experiment with it, and use it as a starting point for their own work.

r001.rationale: The response presents projects as ways to explain ideas and learn through readable code, but does not describe exploring the boundaries of what PyTorch can do.

r002.rationale: It mentions small implementations that others can experiment with, but does not discuss PyTorch puzzles or learning mathematical topics through hands-on play.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them mostly as a way to explore an idea and make it easier for other people to explore it too. If I’m having trouble understanding something, building a small implementation often helps me figure out what’s actually going on. And then, if I can make that implementation clear enough, it becomes something I can share.

With the PyTorch-related projects, a lot of the motivation is making the machinery more explicit. What are the tensors? What are their shapes? How do the pieces fit together? I want the code to be useful, but I also want someone to be able to read it and come away understanding the underlying idea. That’s often the most interesting part for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes using projects to explore ideas and clarify PyTorch machinery, but does not say they explore the boundaries of what PyTorch can do.

r002.rationale: It mentions building small implementations to understand ideas, but does not describe PyTorch puzzles or learning mathematical topics through hands-on play.
